title: Signature Fragment Parsing — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. A deep link carries its target in the fragment — the part after the hash — using conventions like #page=42, #rec=JAH-AT1-000007, or #xywh= for image regions. The resolver parses the fragment into a structured target: kind plus coordinates, and validates it before touching the file. Unknown fragment kinds produce a clear error naming the supported kinds, rather than a silent wrong position. Standardizing fragment parsing means links created by any tool resolve in every tool. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. Lineage: Signature-line counterpart of the public method of the same name, filed as a Signature original in the Signature archive.
provenance: JAH Databases archive-intelligence tools program, lane T2a — Signature original authored for Justin Addam Higgins.

title: Signature Byte-Offset Seeking — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. For large record files, the fastest deep link is a byte offset: an index maps record IDs to their exact position in the file, and the resolver seeks straight there instead of scanning. Offsets are recorded at write time and stay valid as long as the file is append-only, which is why archive files favor append-only layouts. A bounds check guards against stale offsets after compaction, falling back to a scan when the offset no longer lines up. Seek-then-verify gives constant-time record access inside gigabyte files. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. title: Signature In-Document Path Navigation — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. Inside structured documents, deep links use path expressions — collection[3].title, or //section[@id='x'] — to name a node precisely. The resolver evaluates the path step by step against the parsed document, checking types at each step so a list indexed as a dict fails loudly at the right step. Paths can be absolute from the document root or relative to a context node, which keeps links short inside large files. This is JSONPath and XPath thinking applied to archive navigation. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. Lineage: Signature-line counterpart of the public method of the same name, filed as a Signature original in the Signature archive.
provenance: JAH Databases archive-intelligence tools program, lane T2a — Signature original authored for Justin Addam Higgins.

title: Signature Anchor Registry — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. Long documents carry named anchors — section headings, figure captions, record boundaries — registered in a table mapping names to positions when the document is ingested. A deep link naming an anchor resolves through this table in constant time, no matter how large the document. Anchors survive reflow and reformatting because they attach to logical structure, not page numbers. Registries turn 'go to section 4.2' from a scan into a lookup. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. title: Signature Passage Windowing — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. Resolving to a bare offset is rarely enough — users need the surrounding passage for context. Passage windowing expands the resolved position into a window of N characters or lines on each side, snapped to sentence or record boundaries so nothing is cut mid-thought. The window size adapts to the display and the content density. This turns a machine-precise position into a human-readable answer, which is the whole point of a deep link. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. Lineage: Signature-line counterpart of the public method of the same name, filed as a Signature original in the Signature archive.
demo:
text = "Alpha. Beta gamma. Delta epsilon zeta. Eta theta iota kappa."
def window(text, pos, radius=1):
    sents = text.split(". ")
    i = min(range(len(sents)), key=lambda k: abs(text.find(sents[k]) - pos))
    lo, hi = max(0, i - radius), min(len(sents), i + radius + 1)
    return ". ".join(sents[lo:hi])
print(window(text, 20))
